title: Keys in the Relational Model
description: Connect superkeys, candidate keys, primary and alternate identities, and foreign references to precise uniqueness rules and SQL verification.
notes:
## Keys explain which fact is which

Keys identify tuples through attribute values. In a campus Student relation, student_id can identify one student fact even when several students share a name. A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies tuples across the allowed states of the relation. Minimal means no attribute can be removed while retaining that identifying guarantee; it does not mean the shortest-looking name or smallest stored number.

Begin with the intended fact grain. A Student tuple describes one student. An Enrollment tuple can describe one student-course pair. The identity suitable for one relation may be too restrictive for the other. Using student_id alone as the Enrollment key would prevent a student from taking multiple courses under that definition. Keys must distinguish valid facts without ruling out legitimate relationships.

## A current sample cannot establish a guarantee

Suppose a small sample has three students with different names. The names happen to distinguish those rows, but the business model may permit another student with the same name tomorrow. Current uniqueness is evidence about the sample, not proof that student_name is a key for every allowed state. Key reasoning requires the intended constraints or functional dependencies, not only a convenient fixture.

The same caution applies to email. It may be optional, shared, reassigned, or subject to comparison rules that differ from byte equality. A system can deliberately require a nonmissing unique institutional address, but that is a policy to state and enforce. Do not teach every email field as inherently a candidate key simply because the example addresses happen to differ.

## Superkeys allow unnecessary attributes

A superkey is an attribute set that identifies tuples uniquely, possibly with redundant attributes. If student_id already identifies a Student tuple, the pair student_id and student_name remains identifying. Adding the name cannot make two different student identifiers become equal. The larger set is therefore a superkey, but it is not minimal because student_id alone suffices.

Every candidate key is a superkey. Not every superkey is a candidate key. This distinction helps explain why a schema can have many identifying attribute combinations without all of them being suitable declarations of minimal identity. It also avoids confusing a long SELECT list with a better key. Extra descriptive attributes can make references wider and less stable without adding any identifying power.

## Candidate keys can offer alternatives

A relation can have multiple candidate keys. Suppose the documented rules guarantee both a unique nonmissing student_id and a unique nonmissing institutional_number. Each single attribute identifies one student and is minimal under those rules. Choosing one as the primary key does not invalidate the other. Both remain important constraints on which Student states are allowed.

Candidate-key analysis is based on attribute sets. If the only guarantee is that a pair campus_code and local_number is unique, neither component must be unique alone. That pair can be a composite candidate key if neither smaller subset identifies students. A student at another campus can reuse the same local number without violating the pair rule. Treat the pair as one combined identity condition.

## Primary and alternate keys express a choice

The primary key is the candidate key selected as the relation's main declared identifier. The remaining candidate keys are often called alternate keys. In SQL, one PRIMARY KEY constraint can span one or several columns. Appropriate UNIQUE and NOT NULL declarations can enforce other required unique identities. Merely mentioning an alternate identity in documentation does not prevent conflicting writes.

A surrogate identifier can be useful when business labels change or do not reliably distinguish facts. An internal student_id can remain stable when an institutional label changes under a defined policy. It does not automatically enforce every business uniqueness rule. If two records must not claim the same institutional_number, that rule still needs enforcement even when each record receives a different generated internal identifier.

## Composite identities need combined reasoning

For Enrollment(student_id, course_id), a composite key on the pair permits repeated student identifiers across courses and repeated course identifiers across students. It forbids only a repeated identifying pair under the one-enrollment-per-pair policy. Requiring each component to be unique separately would mistakenly restrict both participation patterns and change the represented relationship.

If the system records repeated course attempts, student_id and course_id alone may no longer identify the intended fact. Adding an attempt identifier or attempt number can distinguish occurrences. Do not add score to the key just to make conflicting records appear unique. Two different scores for the same identified attempt are generally a data conflict, not two valid attempts created by the difference in scores.

## Foreign keys refer rather than necessarily identify

A foreign key connects attributes to an allowed referenced key. Enrollment.student_id can refer to Student.student_id while repeating across many enrollments. It need not uniquely identify the enrollment row. The word key therefore appears in concepts with different responsibilities: candidate and primary keys identify local tuples, while foreign keys constrain the validity of references.

An optional single-column foreign reference can be NULL if the definition permits absence. A primary key cannot have missing components. Composite references have additional missing-component considerations and should be described through their actual definitions. A column named advisor_id is not automatically a foreign key; the reference constraint must be declared and supported at the database boundary.

## SQL declarations enforce selected identity rules

A simple student definition can enforce both an internal primary identity and an alternate institutional identity. The name can remain nonunique because different students may share it. These are independent choices, each corresponding to a concrete allowed or rejected situation. Explain them together rather than treating the first integer column as automatically authoritative.

```sql
CREATE TABLE students (
  student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  institutional_number VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  student_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL
);
```

This definition rejects a repeated student_id and a repeated institutional_number. It permits repeated student_name values. It does not establish that every submitted name is factually correct or that an institutional number was issued by the campus. Those external facts and caller permissions require their own validation and trusted decisions.

## Test the identifying guarantee directly

Use two students with the same name to verify that descriptive repetition remains allowed. Try the same primary identity with a different institutional number, then a different primary identity with the same institutional number. Both should be rejected under the declared policy. Test prohibited absence separately so failure does not depend accidentally on a uniqueness conflict elsewhere in the row.

For a composite key, include two rows sharing the first component and two sharing the second while keeping the complete pairs different. Then attempt a repeated pair. These cases distinguish a correct combined constraint from two incorrect single-column constraints. A table containing one row cannot expose the difference, so fixture design matters as much as the number of statements executed.

## Read keys as explicit contracts

An index can support enforcement or lookup performance, but an arbitrary nonunique index is not a candidate-key guarantee. A displayed sort order is also not an identity. A key can support a deterministic tie-breaker in presentation, yet its purpose remains identifying facts independently of their position. Review the actual declared constraints and intended legal states before inferring key properties from a screen or query plan.

A useful key review records the assumed business guarantees before listing attribute sets. Without those assumptions, two apparently different answers may be reasoning about different permitted states. Keep the vocabulary connected: superkeys identify, candidate keys identify minimally, one candidate can be primary, other candidates can be alternate, and foreign keys constrain references. Then separate the conceptual rules from the SQL implementation and its verified scope. This produces designs and queries that follow genuine identities while preserving the legitimate repetition present in campus data.

questions.question_text: In precise candidate-key terminology, what is a key in a relation?
options: Any attribute with a numeric domain
An attribute or minimal set of attributes whose values uniquely identify each tuple in a relation
The first column defined in a CREATE TABLE statement
A synonym for attribute
questions.explanation: A key is defined by its ability to uniquely identify tuples, using a minimal set of attributes.

questions.question_text: Under a schema rule guaranteeing id is unique and nonmissing in every allowed Students state, what is {id}?
options: A foreign key
A candidate key
A composite key only
Not a key at all
questions.explanation: {id} uniquely identifies every tuple and is minimal (no attribute can be removed), making it a candidate key.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes a Super Key from a Candidate Key?
options: A super key must contain exactly one attribute; a candidate key can contain many
A super key is any uniquely-identifying set of attributes (possibly with extras); a candidate key is a MINIMAL such set
They are the same thing
A candidate key can allow duplicate values; a super key cannot
questions.explanation: Every candidate key is a super key, but a candidate key additionally must be minimal — no attribute can be dropped without losing uniqueness.

questions.question_text: If both {email} and {id} are guaranteed nonmissing candidate keys and {id} is chosen as primary, what is {email}?
options: A foreign key
An alternate key
A composite key
It is no longer a valid key
questions.explanation: A candidate key not selected as the primary key is called an alternate key.

questions.question_text: If the enrollment pair is guaranteed unique and neither component alone is guaranteed unique, what is {student_id, course_id}?
options: A candidate key that happens to be a composite key
A foreign key only, not a key at all
A domain constraint
An attribute
questions.explanation: Since the combination is minimal and uniquely identifies each enrollment tuple, it is a candidate key that is composite (made of more than one attribute).

questions.question_text: How do Keys differ conceptually from Relational Integrity rules?
options: They are identical concepts
Keys describe identifying and referencing roles; integrity constraints enforce relevant validity rules, including key uniqueness and references
Integrity rules define which attributes are keys
Keys only matter for foreign key relationships, never for primary keys
questions.explanation: Key roles and integrity requirements are connected rather than disjoint; key constraints are themselves integrity rules.

questions.question_text: Can a foreign key attribute contain NULL even though the primary key it references cannot?
options: No, foreign keys follow the exact same NULL restriction as primary keys
Yes — an optional foreign key like advisor_id can be NULL, since referential integrity and entity integrity are different rules with different NULL requirements
No, this would always violate referential integrity
Yes, but only if the foreign key is also composite
questions.explanation: Entity integrity forbids NULL primary keys, but referential integrity typically permits a NULL foreign key (meaning 'no reference'), unless declared NOT NULL.

questions.question_text: Is {id, name} a candidate key for Students, given that {id} alone already uniquely identifies each tuple?
options: Yes, because it also uniquely identifies tuples
No — it is a super key but not a candidate key, since it is not minimal ({id} alone already suffices)
No, it isn't even a super key
Yes, and it is the only candidate key possible
questions.explanation: {id, name} does identify tuples uniquely, but since {id} alone is sufficient, adding 'name' violates minimality, so {id, name} is a super key, not a candidate key.

questions.question_text: Three sample students have unique names. Does that prove student_name is a candidate key?
options: Yes; any sample proves every future state
No; the allowed-state guarantee must come from the model
Only if sorted
Only if all names are short
questions.explanation: Accidental uniqueness in one state does not establish a key constraint.

questions.question_text: Why is {student_id, student_name} nonminimal when {student_id} is already a key?
options: The identifier can always be removed
Two-column sets never identify
The name can be removed without losing identification
Names cannot be attributes
questions.explanation: Minimality removes redundant identifying attributes.

questions.question_text: Does adding a surrogate primary identifier enforce uniqueness of institutional_number automatically?
options: Yes; every generated id validates all labels
Only if the name matches
No; the institutional rule still needs its own constraint
Only for empty relations
questions.explanation: Internal identity and business uniqueness are separate obligations.

questions.question_text: Must each component of a composite enrollment key be independently unique?
options: Yes; both must be individual keys
Only course_id must be
Only student_id must be
No; uniqueness applies to the combination
questions.explanation: Repeating one component can be a valid different relationship fact.

questions.question_text: What does a foreign student reference in Enrollment need not do?
options: Uniquely identify the enrollment row
Refer to the defined parent key
Follow its nullability policy
Use compatible reference attributes
questions.explanation: One student can be referenced by many enrollment facts.

questions.question_text: What happens to a candidate key not chosen as primary?
options: It becomes invalid
It remains an alternate identifying key
Its attributes must be deleted
It becomes a cursor
questions.explanation: Primary selection does not remove other identity guarantees.

questions.question_text: Which fixture tests that names are descriptive rather than unique identity?
options: One row only
Two rows with the same primary key
Two valid student rows with the same name and different identifiers
No rows and no schema
questions.explanation: The design should accept legitimate repeated names.

questions.question_text: Why should score not be added merely to distinguish conflicting copies of one attempt?
options: Every score is globally unique
Scores cannot be integers
A wider key always fixes data meaning
A different recorded score does not necessarily create a different attempt identity
questions.explanation: The key should represent the actual fact grain.

questions.question_text: Does a nonunique index establish a candidate key?
options: No; it does not guarantee unique identity
Yes; every index is a key
Only when physically first
Only on numeric columns
questions.explanation: Access structures and uniqueness guarantees differ.

questions.question_text: What is a single PRIMARY KEY constraint spanning two columns?
options: Two separate primary keys
One composite primary key
A nullable foreign key automatically
A domain name
questions.explanation: One combined identifying constraint can involve several attributes.

questions.question_text: Which check directly tests alternate institutional identity enforcement?
options: Sort names alphabetically
Count attributes
Insert a new student_id with an already-used institutional_number
Select the first row
questions.explanation: The proposed write challenges the alternate uniqueness rule.

questions.question_text: What defines the correct key for an enrollment attempt relation?
options: The shortest column name
The first displayed column
The most frequent score
The intended occurrence identity and allowed facts
questions.explanation: Fact grain determines which attributes must distinguish tuples.

coding_problems.title: Audit conflicting proposed institutional identities
coding_problems.task: Return institutional_number and proposal_count for proposed institutional numbers occurring more than once. Each proposal is separate; the output is an audit, not a declaration that unobserved future values are unique.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE proposals (proposal_id INT PRIMARY KEY, institutional_number VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL);
constraints: All fixture codes use uppercase canonical spellings with no collation-sensitive differences.
edge_cases: Three conflicting proposals must count as three.
No repeated numbers gives an empty audit.
hints: Group by the proposed alternate identity.
Use HAVING to select conflicting group counts.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT institutional_number, COUNT(*) AS proposal_count FROM proposals GROUP BY institutional_number HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY institutional_number;
coding_problems.explanation: The audit detects current conflicts. An enforced constraint is still needed to protect future accepted data.

coding_problems.title: Enforce primary and alternate student identities
coding_problems.task: Add PRIMARY KEY(student_id) and a UNIQUE constraint named institutional_identity on institutional_number. Both columns are already NOT NULL. Return student_id, institutional_number and student_name. Repeated names must remain valid.
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Add the primary and alternate identity constraints, then return the students.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT NOT NULL, institutional_number VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, student_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.expected:
student_id	institutional_number	student_name
1	S17	Asha
2	S24	Asha
constraints: The initial dataset satisfies both identity guarantees.
edge_cases: Duplicate primary or alternate identity must be rejected independently.
hints: One identity is primary and the other remains unique and required.
Do not impose uniqueness on the descriptive name.
coding_problems.solution_sql:
ALTER TABLE students ADD PRIMARY KEY (student_id), ADD CONSTRAINT institutional_identity UNIQUE (institutional_number);
SELECT student_id, institutional_number, student_name FROM students ORDER BY student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The two constraints enforce independent identifying rules while the schema permits legitimate repeated student names.

validation_cases.expected:
student_id	institutional_number	student_name
2	S2	Mira
9	S9	Mira
